CHAPTER 4 · LEARNING AREA 4

CHAPTER 4 · LEARNING AREA 4 · MARCH

Similarity

A photo can be enlarged without the faces getting wider. A hiking map shows the Elbe Sandstone Mountains at a scale of 1 : 25,000, and still every angle is right. Figures that look the same but are different sizes are called similar. You enlarge figures with a central dilation, measure the height of a tree from its shadow and find out why a giant twice as tall as you would not be twice but eight times as heavy.

14 LESSONS4 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • dilate figures from a centre, calculate with the scale factor and the scale
  • recognise similar figures and apply the main similarity theorem
  • work out missing lengths with ratios, find heights from shadows
  • know how areas ($k^2$) and volumes ($k^3$) change; congruence as the special case $k = 1$

$300\,\text{cm} = 3\,\text{m}$

Both divided by 6: $2 : 3$

Solve $\dfrac{x}{4} = \dfrac{6}{8}$.

$x = 4 \cdot 0.75 = 3$

In a triangle, $\alpha = 50^\circ$ and $\beta = 70^\circ$. How big is $\gamma$?

$180^\circ - 120^\circ = 60^\circ$

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Central dilation and scale

A projector throws a small picture onto the screen. All the light rays come from one point, the lens. If the screen is twice as far from the lens as the small picture, every segment becomes twice as long. That is a central dilation.

KEY POINT · CENTRAL DILATION

In a central dilation with the centre $Z$ and the scale factor $k$ ($k > 0$), the image point $P'$ lies on the ray $ZP$, and $\overline{ZP'} = k \cdot \overline{ZP}$.

$k > 1$: enlargement · $0 < k < 1$: reduction · $k = 1$: image and original are the same.

Every image segment is $k$ times as long as its original segment and parallel to it. All the angles stay the same.

Scale $1 : n$: 1 cm on the map is $n$ cm in reality.

Constructing: draw a ray from $Z$ through every vertex, measure the distance, multiply by $k$ and mark it off on the ray.

Enlargement as a scale: 50 : 1 means 50 mm in the picture are 1 mm in reality, for example for an insect.

INTERACTIVE · DILATING FROM THE CENTRE

Drag the centre and the vertices, change $k$. Compare the lengths, the angles and the areas.

EXAMPLE 1 · IN THE COORDINATE SYSTEM

Dilate the triangle $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 1)$, $C(2, 3)$ from the origin with $k = 2$.

With the centre $(0, 0)$, both coordinates are multiplied by $k$: $A'(2, 2)$, $B'(8, 2)$, $C'(4, 6)$.

All the sides are twice as long, the angles stay the same. $\overline{A'B'} = 6$ instead of $\overline{AB} = 3$.

EXAMPLE 2 · THE HIKING MAP

On a map at a scale of 1 : 25,000, a path is 6 cm long. How long is it in reality? How long would 4 km be on the map?

$6\,\text{cm} \cdot 25{,}000 = 150{,}000\,\text{cm} = 1.5\,\text{km}$. The other way round: $4\,\text{km} = 400{,}000\,\text{cm}$, divided by 25,000 gives 16 cm.

The path is 1.5 km long. 4 km are 16 cm on the map.

EXERCISES

Dilate the triangle $A(2, 1)$, $B(5, 2)$, $C(3, 4)$ from the origin with $k = 1.5$. Give the image points and draw.

$A'(3, 1.5)$, $B'(7.5, 3)$, $C'(4.5, 6)$

a) Map 1 : 50,000, a distance of 3 cm: how long in reality?   b) Building plan 1 : 200, a room 4.5 m long: how long on the plan?   c) Model car 1 : 18, the model is 25 cm long: how long is the car?

a) 1.5 km   b) 2.25 cm   c) 450 cm = 4.5 m

A segment is 6 cm long, its image segment 4.5 cm. How big is the scale factor? Is it an enlargement or a reduction?

$k = \tfrac{4.5}{6} = 0.75$: a reduction.

A picture 24 cm wide and 18 cm high appears 3 m wide on the screen. How big is the scale factor? How high is the picture on the screen?

$k = \tfrac{300}{24} = 12.5$. Height: $12.5 \cdot 18\,\text{cm} = 225\,\text{cm} = 2.25\,\text{m}$.

In a central dilation, $A(1, 2)$ is mapped to $A'(3, 6)$ and $B(3, 1)$ to $B'(9, 3)$. Find the centre and the scale factor.

The lines $AA'$ and $BB'$ both pass through the origin: $Z(0, 0)$. All the coordinates are tripled: $k = 3$.

TEST YOURSELF!

A segment 4 cm long is dilated with $k = 3$. How long is the image segment?

12 cm

Map 1 : 100,000: how many kilometres are 5 cm?

$500{,}000\,\text{cm} = 5\,\text{km}$

A segment 10 cm long has an image segment 4 cm long. How big is $k$?

$k = \tfrac{4}{10} = 0.4$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Similar figures

A photo in the format 10 × 15 and one in the format 20 × 30 show the same picture. All the lengths are doubled, all the angles the same. A photo in the format 10 × 20, on the other hand, would be distorted. When are two figures really similar?

KEY POINT · SIMILARITY

Two figures are similar if one is obtained from the other by a central dilation, possibly together with a translation, a rotation or a reflection. Then corresponding angles are equal, and corresponding sides have the same ratio: $\dfrac{a'}{a} = \dfrac{b'}{b} = \dfrac{c'}{c} = k$.

Main similarity theorem: if two triangles agree in two angles, then they are similar.

Only for triangles: a square and a long rectangle have the same angles but are not similar. For polygons the ratios of the sides must match too.

Shadows: at the same time the sun’s rays fall in parallel. Object, shadow and ray form similar triangles.

INTERACTIVE · BUILDING A SIMILAR TRIANGLE

On the grid, build a triangle that is similar to the given one. The widget compares the angles and the ratios of the sides.

INTERACTIVE · HEIGHTS FROM SHADOWS

A stick and a tree cast shadows at the same time. The two triangles are similar.

EXAMPLE 3 · MISSING SIDES

A triangle has the sides $a = 4\,\text{cm}$, $b = 5\,\text{cm}$, $c = 6\,\text{cm}$. In a similar triangle, $a' = 6\,\text{cm}$. Work out $b'$ and $c'$.

$k = \tfrac{a'}{a} = \tfrac{6}{4} = 1.5$. Then $b' = 1.5 \cdot 5\,\text{cm} = 7.5\,\text{cm}$ and $c' = 1.5 \cdot 6\,\text{cm} = 9\,\text{cm}$.

$b' = 7.5\,\text{cm}$, $c' = 9\,\text{cm}$

EXAMPLE 4 · HOW TALL IS THE TREE?

A person 1.60 m tall casts a shadow 2 m long. At the same time a tree casts a shadow 15 m long.

The triangles person–shadow and tree–shadow are similar: $\dfrac{h}{15\,\text{m}} = \dfrac{1.6\,\text{m}}{2\,\text{m}}$, so $h = 15\,\text{m} \cdot 0.8 = 12\,\text{m}$.

The tree is 12 m tall.

EXERCISES

Are the triangles similar? a) Triangle 1 has the angles $40^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, triangle 2 the angles $40^\circ$ and $80^\circ$.   b) Triangle 1: $50^\circ$ and $60^\circ$, triangle 2: $50^\circ$ and $80^\circ$.

a) The third angles are $80^\circ$ and $60^\circ$: both have $40^\circ$, $60^\circ$, $80^\circ$. Similar.   b) $50^\circ$, $60^\circ$, $70^\circ$ against $50^\circ$, $80^\circ$, $50^\circ$: not similar.

Are the rectangles similar? a) 3 cm × 5 cm and 6 cm × 10 cm   b) 4 cm × 6 cm and 6 cm × 8 cm

a) yes, $k = 2$   b) no: $\tfrac{6}{4} = 1.5$, but $\tfrac{8}{6} \approx 1.33$

A triangle has the sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm. In a similar triangle the longest side is 7.5 cm. How long are the other two sides?

$k = \tfrac{7.5}{5} = 1.5$: 4.5 cm and 6 cm.

A stick 1 m long casts a shadow 0.80 m long, a flagpole at the same time one 9.60 m long. How tall is the pole?

$h = 9.6\,\text{m} \cdot \tfrac{1}{0.8} = 12\,\text{m}$

Foresters measure the heights of trees with an isosceles right-angled triangle: they sight along the hypotenuse and step back until they see the top of the tree. A forester then stands 18 m from the tree, her eyes 1.60 m above the ground. How tall is the tree? Try it in the widget in the forester’s triangle mode.

The big triangle is also isosceles and right-angled: above eye level, the tree is as tall as the distance is long, so 18 m. Add the eye height: 19.60 m.

TEST YOURSELF!

Two triangles are similar with $a = 2\,\text{cm}$, $a' = 5\,\text{cm}$ and $b = 4\,\text{cm}$. How long is $b'$?

$k = 2.5$, $b' = 10\,\text{cm}$

A stick 2 m long casts a shadow 3 m long, a tower one 45 m long. How tall is the tower?

$45 \cdot \tfrac{2}{3} = 30$, so 30 m.

How many equal angles are enough for two triangles to be similar?

Two, because then the third one is equal too.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Lengths, areas and volumes

For a cube with double the edge length you need not 2 but 8 small cubes. Each face consists of 4 small squares. If every length is doubled, every area becomes four times as big, and the volume eight times as big.

KEY POINT · k, k² AND k³

If two figures or solids are similar with the scale factor $k$, then:

Lengths: $a' = k \cdot a \qquad$ Areas: $A' = k^2 \cdot A \qquad$ Volumes: $V' = k^3 \cdot V$

Double the length: four times the area, eight times the volume. Triple the length: nine times the area, 27 times the volume.

There are no giants: the weight grows with the volume ($k^3$), the strength of the bones only with their cross-sectional area ($k^2$).

Backwards: if an area is 9 times as big, $k = 3$. If a volume is 8 times as big, $k = 2$.

INTERACTIVE · GULLIVER AMONG THE LILLIPUTIANS

Change $k$ and compare: lengths times $k$, areas times $k^2$, volumes times $k^3$.

EXAMPLE 5 · THE MODEL HOUSE

A model house at a scale of 1 : 50 has a floor area of $300\,\text{cm}^2$ and a volume of $3000\,\text{cm}^3$. How big are the floor area and the volume of the real house?

$k = 50$: area times $50^2 = 2500$, volume times $50^3 = 125{,}000$.

$300\,\text{cm}^2 \cdot 2500 = 750{,}000\,\text{cm}^2 = 75\,\text{m}^2$, $\;3000\,\text{cm}^3 \cdot 125{,}000 = 375{,}000{,}000\,\text{cm}^3 = 375\,\text{m}^3$

$75\,\text{m}^2$ of floor area and $375\,\text{m}^3$ of enclosed space.

EXAMPLE 6 · PAINT AND WEIGHT

A wooden cube with an edge length of 10 cm is painted with 30 ml of paint and weighs 700 g. What about a cube with an edge length of 30 cm?

$k = 3$. Paint for the surface: $3^2 = 9$ times as much, 270 ml. Weight: $3^3 = 27$ times as much, 18,900 g.

270 ml of paint, 18.9 kg.

EXERCISES

A square with a side length of 4 cm is dilated with $k = 2.5$. Work out the side length, the perimeter and the area before and after.

Side 4 cm → 10 cm, perimeter 16 cm → 40 cm (times $k$), area $16\,\text{cm}^2$ → $100\,\text{cm}^2$ (times $k^2 = 6.25$).

A figure has an area of $12\,\text{cm}^2$, a solid a volume of $5\,\text{cm}^3$. Both are dilated with $k = 3$. How big are the area and the volume afterwards?

$12 \cdot 9 = 108\,\text{cm}^2$ and $5 \cdot 27 = 135\,\text{cm}^3$

A pizza with a diameter of 26 cm costs €8, one with 32 cm costs €11. What percentage more pizza do you get with the big one? Is it worth it?

$k = \tfrac{32}{26} \approx 1.23$, $k^2 \approx 1.51$: about 51% more pizza for $\tfrac{11}{8} = 1.375$, so 37.5% more money. The big one is worth it.

Gulliver is 12 times as tall as a Lilliputian. How many Lilliputian portions must he eat if hunger grows with volume? How many Lilliputian shirts are needed for his shirt if the fabric grows with area?

Portions: $12^3 = 1728$. Fabric: $12^2 = 144$ shirts.

A bronze statue is 2 m high and weighs 800 kg. A copy made of the same bronze is 50 cm high. How heavy is it?

$k = \tfrac{0.5}{2} = 0.25$, $k^3 = \tfrac{1}{64}$. $800\,\text{kg} : 64 = 12.5\,\text{kg}$.

TEST YOURSELF!

A figure is dilated with $k = 4$. How many times as big does its area become?

$4^2 = 16$

A solid with $10\,\text{cm}^3$ is dilated with $k = 2$. How big is the volume afterwards?

$10 \cdot 8 = 80$

In an enlargement the area becomes 25 times as big. How big is $k$?

$k^2 = 25$, $k = 5$

UNIT 42 LESSONS

4Congruence as a special case

Two tiles from the same pack can be laid exactly on top of each other. They are not only similar but also the same size. That is a similarity with the scale factor $k = 1$.

KEY POINT · CONGRUENCE

Figures that can be made to coincide by a translation, a rotation or a reflection are called congruent.

Congruence is the special case of similarity with $k = 1$: corresponding angles and corresponding sides are equal.

Congruence criteria for triangles: two triangles are congruent if they agree in three sides (SSS), in two sides and the included angle (SAS), in one side and two angles (ASA) or in two sides and the angle opposite the longer side (SsA).

Similar but not congruent: a photo and its enlargement.

AAA is not a congruence criterion: three equal angles only give similar triangles, by the main similarity theorem.

INTERACTIVE · WHICH PIECES FIX A TRIANGLE?

Choose what is given and change the values. Do you get exactly one triangle, none or two?

EXAMPLE 7 · CONGRUENT OR ONLY SIMILAR?

Triangle 1: $a = 3\,\text{cm}$, $b = 4\,\text{cm}$, $\gamma = 90^\circ$. Triangle 2: $a = 4\,\text{cm}$, $b = 3\,\text{cm}$, $\gamma = 90^\circ$. Triangle 3: $a = 6\,\text{cm}$, $b = 8\,\text{cm}$, $\gamma = 90^\circ$.

1 and 2 agree in two sides and the included right angle (SAS), only reflected: congruent. Triangle 3 has sides twice as long: similar with $k = 2$.

1 and 2 are congruent, 3 is only similar to both.

EXAMPLE 8 · WHICH CRITERION FITS?

Of a triangle you know $c = 5\,\text{cm}$, $\alpha = 40^\circ$ and $\beta = 60^\circ$. Is it fixed uniquely?

The side $c$ lies between the angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$: congruence criterion ASA.

Yes, all triangles with these values are congruent.

EXERCISES

Rectangles: A 2 cm × 3 cm, B 3 cm × 2 cm, C 4 cm × 6 cm, D 2 cm × 4 cm. Which are congruent, which only similar?

A and B are congruent (rotated). C is similar to A and B with $k = 2$. D is similar to none of them.

Which congruence criterion fits? a) $a = 4$, $b = 5$, $c = 6$   b) $b = 5$, $c = 6$, $\alpha = 50^\circ$   c) $c = 7$, $\alpha = 30^\circ$, $\beta = 80^\circ$   d) $a = 6$, $b = 4$, $\alpha = 70^\circ$

a) SSS   b) SAS ($\alpha$ lies between $b$ and $c$)   c) ASA   d) SsA ($\alpha$ lies opposite the longer side $a$)

Show with two drawings that three equal angles do not fix a triangle uniquely.

For example two equilateral triangles with side lengths of 2 cm and 5 cm: both have three angles of $60^\circ$, are similar, but not congruent.

Construct triangles with $b = 4\,\text{cm}$, $c = 5\,\text{cm}$ and $\beta = 40^\circ$. How many different triangles are there? Why does no congruence criterion apply here?

The angle $\beta$ lies opposite the shorter side $b$. The circle around $A$ with 4 cm cuts the free arm twice: two different triangles. SsA requires the angle to lie opposite the longer side.

TEST YOURSELF!

What scale factor do congruent figures have?

$k = 1$

Which information always fixes a triangle uniquely?

Three sides (SSS). With two sides and an angle it depends on where the angle lies.

Two triangles are congruent. In the first one a side is 7 cm long. How long is the corresponding side in the second one?

Also 7 cm.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

On a town map at a scale of 1 : 20,000, your way to school is 7.5 cm long. How long is it in reality?

$7.5 \cdot 20{,}000\,\text{cm} = 150{,}000\,\text{cm} = 1.5\,\text{km}$

Connect with chapter 3.1: all circles are similar to each other. A circle with $r = 3\,\text{cm}$ is dilated with $k = 2$. How do the circumference and the area change?

Circumference: $6\pi \to 12\pi$, times 2. Area: $9\pi \to 36\pi$, times 4.

Connect with chapter 3.2: a tin is doubled in radius and height. How many times as much fits into it, how many times as much sheet metal does it need?

Volume times $2^3 = 8$, sheet metal (surface area) times $2^2 = 4$.

An A4 sheet is 21.0 cm × 29.7 cm, an A5 sheet 14.8 cm × 21.0 cm. Are the two similar? How are their areas related?

$\tfrac{29.7}{21.0} \approx 1.414$ and $\tfrac{21.0}{14.8} \approx 1.419$: almost equal, the sheets are similar (apart from rounding). A5 has half the area of A4: $623.7\,\text{cm}^2$ against $310.8\,\text{cm}^2$.

EXCURSIONHISTORY AND BIOLOGY

Why there are no giants

In 1638, Galileo Galilei wrote in his Discorsi that giants cannot simply be enlarged people. If a person were ten times as tall, he would weigh $10^3 = 1000$ times as much. But his bones would only carry as much as their cross-section allows, and that grows only $10^2 = 100$ times. The bones would break. That is why elephants have such thick legs and ants such thin ones.

Almost ninety years later, Jonathan Swift played with this: in Gulliver’s Travels (1726) the scholars of Lilliput measure that Gulliver is twelve times as tall and work out from this how much he must eat. Many editions say 1724 portions there. The correct number would be $12^3 = 1728$.

Sources: G. Galilei, Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze, Leiden 1638, second day. J. Swift, Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World (Gulliver’s Travels), London 1726, part I, chapter 3.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

CENTRAL DILATION

$\overline{ZP'} = k \cdot \overline{ZP}$, image segments parallel and $k$ times as long, angles equal; scale $1 : n$

1 : 25,000: 6 cm are 1.5 km

SIMILARITY

equal angles, equal ratios of sides; triangles: two equal angles are enough

Shadow: $\tfrac{h}{15} = \tfrac{1.6}{2}$, $h = 12\,\text{m}$

k · k² · k³

lengths times $k$, areas times $k^2$, volumes times $k^3$

$k = 2$: area ×4, volume ×8

CONGRUENCE

similarity with $k = 1$; congruence criteria SSS, SAS, ASA, SsA

AAA only fixes the shape

A segment 3 cm long is dilated with $k = 2.5$. How long does it become?

7.5 cm

A solid is dilated with $k = 3$. How many times as big does its volume become?

$3^3 = 27$

One triangle has the angles $30^\circ$ and $70^\circ$, another $70^\circ$ and $80^\circ$. Are they similar?

The third angle is $80^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ respectively: both have $30^\circ$, $70^\circ$, $80^\circ$.

ROUND 2 · THINK IT THROUGH

Map 1 : 40,000, a distance of 6 cm. How many kilometres is that?

$240{,}000\,\text{cm} = 2.4\,\text{km}$

A stick 1.5 m high casts a shadow 2 m long, a house at the same time one 24 m long. How tall is the house?

$24 \cdot 0.75 = 18$, so 18 m.

A wooden figure 30 cm high weighs 5.4 kg. A model made of the same wood is 10 cm high. How many grams does it weigh?

$k = \tfrac{1}{3}$, $k^3 = \tfrac{1}{27}$: $5400\,\text{g} : 27 = 200\,\text{g}$
